sections.h: 2 Corinthians 1–5: comfort, the new covenant and reconciliation
sections.b: The first five chapters open with a blessing for the God of all comfort and the story of Paul's near-death in Asia (1:3–11). Paul defends his changed travel plans (1:12–2:4), asks the church to forgive an offender (2:5–11), and tells of his anxious search for Titus (2:12–13). He then sets out the ministry of the new covenant, the letter written on hearts and the veil of Moses (2:14–4:6), the treasure in clay pots (4:7–18), the hope of a heavenly dwelling (5:1–10), and the ministry of reconciliation (5:11–21).

common: Most scholars agree that Paul wrote 2 Corinthians, at about AD 55–56 from Macedonia.
uncommon: A minority hold that the tearful letter is 1 Corinthians and that Paul made no intermediate painful visit.

sections.h: The letter written on hearts (2 Corinthians 3)
sections.b: Paul says the Corinthians are a letter of Christ, written "not in ink but by the Spirit of the living God, not on stone tablets but on tablets that are hearts of flesh." He says God made him able to serve "a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit," and compares the ministry carved on stone with the ministry of the Spirit. The phrase "new covenant" comes from Jeremiah 31:31–34, and "hearts of flesh" from Ezekiel 36:26. Paul calls the Mosaic covenant "old" in 3:14, the only place in the New Testament that uses the phrase.

common: The new covenant of 2 Corinthians 3 is the one promised in Jeremiah 31.
uncommon: Some "Paul within Judaism" scholars hold that Paul says nothing in 2 Corinthians 3 about the covenant with Israel, only about his own ministry among Gentiles.

sections.h: Moses, the glory and the veil (2 Corinthians 3:7–18)
sections.b: Paul retells Exodus 34 to compare two ministries. The glory of Moses's face was "being set aside" and he covered it; today a veil lies on the heart of those who read Moses; when someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. Paul adds to Exodus: he says why Moses wore the veil and says the glory was being set aside, which Exodus does not say. All believers, with unveiled faces, look at the Lord's glory as in a mirror and are changed into his image.

common: Paul's picture of the veil on the reading of Moses is a picture of a hardness that remains until a person turns to the Lord.
uncommon: A reading takes the veil as Moses's mercy: God's glory would have destroyed a stiff-necked people (Hafemann).

sections.b: Paul says everything is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave the apostles the ministry of reconciliation: in Christ, God was reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning their trespasses to them. The apostles are ambassadors who beg on Christ's behalf, "Be reconciled to God." The paragraph ends with the exchange of 5:21: God made the sinless one to be sin for us, so that we could become the righteousness of God in him.

common: God is the one who reconciles, and the human being is the one reconciled.
uncommon: Some read "the world" in 5:19 as all people without exception, and hold that the verse supports a hope that all will be reconciled.

sections.h: Away from the body, at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:1–10)
sections.b: Paul compares the body to a tent and says that if it is taken down, God has a building ready, a house not made by hands. He groans, wishing to be "dressed over" and not unclothed, and says he is confident, even preferring "to be away from the body and at home with the Lord." The text does not say whether he expects a body at death or only at Christ's return, and scholars and churches differ.

common: Paul expects to be with the Lord when he dies.
uncommon: Some hold that Paul changed his view between 1 Corinthians 15 and 2 Corinthians 5 after nearly dying in Asia (Dodd).

sections.h: The judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10)
sections.b: Paul says that all must be shown openly before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for the things done through the body, according to what he did, whether good or bad. The word is the Greek bema, the platform from which a Roman official gave a verdict, and Corinth had one. Paul uses the verse to explain his ambition to please Christ and his sincere way of working (5:9, 11). Churches differ on whether the judgment is a test of salvation, a reward for believers, or both.

Titus first appears in 2 Corinthians at 2:13, when Paul could not rest at Troas because he did not find his brother Titus there. Paul most likely had sent Titus to Corinth with the tearful letter and was waiting for his news. He left Troas for Macedonia to meet him. The story is taken up again at 7:5–16.

The first five chapters show a Roman colony where honor and patronage mattered. Paul's changed travel plans were read as a broken promise, letters of recommendation counted for much (3:1), and the "judgment seat" (bema) of 5:10 was a familiar sight in the forum, where Gallio had sat in judgment (Acts 18:12–17). The letter is addressed also to "all the saints throughout Achaia" (1:1), such as the believers at Cenchreae.

sections.h: Paul's account of himself in 2 Corinthians 1–5
sections.b: In these chapters Paul speaks of his near-death in Asia (1:8–11), his anxiety about Corinth (2:1–13), his picture of Christ's victory parade (2:14), in which he may see himself as a captive (the Plain leaves that open), and his body as a clay pot (4:7). He defends his sincerity against the charge of fickleness and says he has no need for letters of recommendation. He says he knows no one, and Christ no longer, "by the flesh" (5:16).

Paul says that God comforts us in all our trouble so that we can comfort others (1:3–7). He carries "the dying of Jesus" in his body so that Jesus's life may be shown in it (4:10–12), and he counts present trouble as slight beside an eternal glory (4:17). The same pattern of weakness and power returns in 12:9–10.

sections.h: The God who raises the dead (2 Corinthians 1:9; 4:14; 5:1–10)
sections.b: Paul says his near-death taught him to trust "God, who raises the dead" (1:9), and that the one who raised the Lord Jesus will raise him and the Corinthians together (4:14). He speaks of a heavenly building and of being "dressed over" with it so that what is mortal is swallowed up by life (5:1–4).

"If anyone is in Christ: new creation!" Paul has no verb here, and the saying has been read of the individual, the church and the world. The background is Isaiah's promise of new things (Isaiah 43:19; 65:17). In Galatians 6:15 he says that what counts is "a new creation," not circumcision or uncircumcision. In 4:6 the same God who said "light" has shone in the heart.

sections.h: One for all, and the exchange (2 Corinthians 5:14–21)
sections.b: Paul says that one died for all, and so all died (5:14). In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning trespasses to them (5:19). And God made the one who did not know sin to be sin for us, so that in him we could become the righteousness of God (5:21). The text has been read as sin offering, as substitution, as exchange, and as participation in Christ.

After the church had punished an offender, Paul asked it to forgive and comfort him so that he would not be swallowed up by too much grief, and so that Satan would not take advantage. Paul joins in the forgiveness: "Anyone you forgive anything, I forgive too." The Latin text's "in the person of Christ" for "before the face of Christ" (2:10) has been used for the priest's absolution.

sections.h: Discipline that ends in restoration (2 Corinthians 2:5–11)
sections.b: Paul's advice to Corinth after an offender had been punished by the majority is to forgive him, comfort him and confirm love for him, lest he be overwhelmed by sorrow. It shows that the aim of discipline is to bring a person back. Whether the offender is the man of 1 Corinthians 5 is disputed.

Satan wants to take advantage of a church that will not forgive (2:11). He is "the god of this age," who has blinded the minds of unbelievers (4:4). Some early Christians read "God" as the subject of the blinding, to guard against heretics who made the Creator an evil god. Paul names Satan again in 11:3, 11:14 and 12:7.

The Spirit is God's seal and down payment in believers' hearts (1:22; 5:5), the writer of the letter on hearts (3:3), the giver of life (3:6), and the Lord who gives freedom (3:17). Believers are changed into the Lord's image "from the Lord, who is the Spirit" (3:18).

The word glory comes ten times in chapter 3. The ministry of Moses came with glory that was being set aside. The ministry of the Spirit has more. Believers look at the Lord's glory as in a mirror and are changed from glory to glory (3:18). The light of the knowledge of God's glory shines in the face of Christ (4:6). A present trouble that is slight produces a glory beyond measure that lasts forever (4:17).

Eastern writers, Gregory of Nyssa among them, read the change "from glory to glory" as the soul's endless growth toward God, the heart of the idea of theosis. Catholic teaching speaks of divinization by grace. Other traditions speak of sanctification, the restoration of God's image, or growth in perfect love.

Paul calls his conscience as witness to his sincerity (1:12) and commends himself "to every human conscience" (4:2) and to the Corinthians' consciences (5:11). The conscience is the inner witness, but God is the final judge (compare 1 Corinthians 4:4).

Paul calls himself a servant of a new covenant (3:6) and speaks of the old covenant being read when Moses is read aloud (3:14). The promises of God are all "Yes" in Christ (1:20). The seal and down payment of the Spirit (1:22) show that the age of the promise has begun.

Paul says the letter kills and the Spirit gives life. He speaks of a ministry of death and condemnation engraved on stones, which had glory. Readings of "the letter" include the literal sense of Scripture, the Law without grace, the condemning Law, the Sinai covenant, and a contrast with his rivals' ministry. Paul still calls the Law holy elsewhere (Romans 7:12).

sections.h: Christ the image of God (2 Corinthians 4:4)
sections.b: Paul says Christ is "the image of God," and that believers are being changed into that same image (3:18). The thought joins Genesis 1:26–27, where humans are made in God's image, with the picture of Christ as the true Adam. Colossians 1:15 says the same of Christ.

Paul says that the minds of Israel were hardened (using the callus word of Romans 11:7, 25) and that a veil lies on their heart when Moses is read. The hardening is not final: the veil is taken away whenever someone turns to the Lord (3:16). Paul writes of his own people with grief and hope in Romans 9–11.

sections.h: The old covenant and the veil (2 Corinthians 3)
sections.b: Chapter 3 is a main text in the debate over whether the covenant with Israel at Sinai is ended. Paul calls it "old" in 3:14, speaks of a veil on the reading of Moses, and of a new covenant in the Spirit. Churches have read this as supersession, as fulfillment, or as about Paul's own ministry; see the cards at 3:6 and 3:14.

sections.h: Father, Son and Spirit in 2 Corinthians 1–5
sections.b: God establishes and anoints us in Christ and seals us with the Spirit (1:21–22). "The Lord is the Spirit" (3:17), with "the Spirit of the Lord" in the same verse, shows how closely Paul links Christ and the Spirit without erasing the difference. The closing blessing (13:14) names the three together.

Paul calls himself an apostle "through the will of God" (1:1) and says that he needs no letters of recommendation, since the church itself is his letter (3:1–3). He is a slave of the Corinthians for Jesus's sake (4:5) and an ambassador for Christ (5:20). His sufferings are the mark of his ministry, not a sign against it.

Paul says he was weighed down beyond his power in the province of Asia, whose capital was Ephesus, and had in himself the verdict of death. He does not say what happened. Some link it to the riot of Acts 19, to a prison, or to an illness.

Paul pictures the apostles in the victory parade of Christ, using the Roman triumph, the highest public honor Rome could give a general. Interpreters differ on whether he sees himself as a captive led in the parade, as a sharer in the victory, or as one who spreads the incense; the Plain leaves this open (see the note at 2:14). The picture takes the language of a Roman public spectacle and gives it to a different king.
